subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff in Human Judgment
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Bias-Variance Tradeoff in Human Judgment.

hook.text: A weather model that perfectly predicts last year's weather often fails tomorrow. It memorized, not learned.

buildup.text: In machine learning, the bias-variance tradeoff shows that flexibility creates accuracy on old data but errors on new.

discovery.text: Human heuristics are biased but low-variance. They give consistent answers that perform well on average.

twist.text: A complex thinker who tries to weight everything may overfit to today's situation and fail tomorrow.

climax.text: Some bias is the cost of being robust. A slightly wrong but consistent rule beats a precise but fragile one.

punchline.text: A little bias buys a lot of stability.

quiz.question: What is the tradeoff in human heuristics?
options: Some bias in exchange for consistent, robust performance

details.summary: The bias-variance tradeoff in human judgment mirrors the statistical concept: simple heuristics have high bias but low variance, while complex strategies have low bias but high variance. When prediction error is dominated by variance, simpler strategies win overall.
details.whyItMatters: This tradeoff explains why experts who use simple rules sometimes outperform algorithmic models. In noisy environments with limited data, the variance reduction from simplicity more than compensates for the bias introduced by ignoring available.
takeaways: Simple heuristics trade increased bias for decreased variance in judgments
High-variance complex models overfit to noise in small samples
The optimal complexity depends on the noise level and sample size

faq.question: How does the bias-variance tradeoff apply to human decision-making?
faq.answer: A doctor who uses three symptoms to diagnose has a biased model that misses some nuance. But the model is stable and consistent. A doctor who considers twenty factors might be more accurate on average but varies widely from case to case, sometimes badly wrong.

faq.question: What determines whether a simple or complex judgment strategy is better?
faq.answer: The amount of data available, the noise level in the environment, and how stable the relationships are. When data is plentiful and relationships are stable, complex models win. When data is scarce and noisy, simple models win by avoiding overfitting.
